tracks.title: Sharing the road with driverless cars
tracks.note: Phil과 Pippa가 운전자 없는 자율주행차(robotaxi)와 보행자·자전거가 어떻게 '소통'할지 이야기해요. 사람 운전자와는 눈을 마주치고 손을 흔들지만, 운전석이 비어 있으면? 그리고 한국은 무단횡단(jaywalking)이 드물어서 자율주행차에 잘 맞는 나라라는 이야기도 나와요! 1회차는 대략적인 내용만, 2회차는 스크립트를 보면서 들어요.

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: Hello, this is 6 Minute English from BBC Learning English.

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: I'm Phil.

transcript.speaker: Pippa
transcript.text: And I'm Pippa.

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: Here at 6 Minute English, we love discussing new tech.

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: One of the most controversial technologies of recent years is driverless cars, also known as self-driving cars, autonomous cars or robotaxis.

transcript.speaker: Pippa
transcript.text: Many people say they wouldn't feel safe in a car without a human driver, but there are concerns from other road users too – pedestrians, runners and cyclists.

transcript.speaker: Pippa
transcript.text: How will driverless cars interact with them?

transcript.speaker: Pippa
transcript.text: It's a problem Professor Stephen Brewster, from Glasgow University, has been working on.

transcript.speaker: Pippa
transcript.text: He explained more to BBC World Service programme Tech Life.

transcript.speaker: Stephen Brewster
transcript.text: If you're outside a vehicle right now, you can see the driver inside the vehicle, you can wave to them, they can see you, you can make eye contact.

transcript.speaker: Stephen Brewster
transcript.text: But when you come to an autonomous vehicle, there's no person in the driving seat, so how do you negotiate whether they're going to go, whether they're going to let you go?

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: On my walk to work, I need to cross the road.

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: Usually, a driver makes eye contact with me.

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: They look directly into my eyes and then wave me across.

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: To wave means to raise your hand and move it from side to side.

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: It's a gesture for saying hello, or a way of telling a person to do something.

transcript.speaker: Pippa
transcript.text: Luckily, Phil, you usually arrive safely at work and as yet there are no driverless cars in London.

transcript.speaker: Pippa
transcript.text: But, Phil, how would you feel about crossing that road in front of a robotaxi?

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: Well, maybe a little bit nervous.

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: I might wait for it to go and go behind it or something.

transcript.speaker: Pippa
transcript.text: Mmm... yeah, I get that.

transcript.speaker: Pippa
transcript.text: I think maybe as we get more used to these technologies, we'll get more used to how to deal with them and when to cross.

transcript.speaker: Pippa
transcript.text: But in this episode, we investigate the tech helping driverless cars communicate on the roads.

transcript.speaker: Pippa
transcript.text: We'll learn some useful new words and phrases, and as usual you'll find all the vocabulary on our website, bbclearningenglish.com.

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: But first, I have a question for you, Pippa.

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: As you mentioned, we don't have self-driving cars here in London yet.

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: So, which was the first city to have fully driverless robotaxis on the streets?

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: Was it: a) Philadelphia, b) Phoenix, or c) San Francisco?

transcript.speaker: Pippa
transcript.text: I'm going to say b) Phoenix because I think it's quite a car-friendly city.

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: OK.

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: Well, we will find out the answer, but at the end of the programme.

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: Because accidents are often caused by not seeing the oncoming danger, Professor Brewster wants to make driverless cars more visible.

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: He discussed his work with BBC Tech Life's presenter Chris Vallance.

transcript.speaker: Chris Vallance
transcript.text: What kind of signals worked in terms of alerting pedestrians and runners and cyclists to the intentions of the vehicle?

transcript.speaker: Stephen Brewster
transcript.text: We tested two things.

transcript.speaker: Stephen Brewster
transcript.text: We tested animations and fixed, coloured light rings.

transcript.speaker: Stephen Brewster
transcript.text: The animations – they work well for pedestrians, but when it came to runners and cyclists, they have much less time to make their decisions, so if you do a quick glance at a vehicle, you don't really see the animation.

transcript.speaker: Pippa
transcript.text: It's important to alert people to driverless cars.

transcript.speaker: Pippa
transcript.text: To alert somebody means to warn them about a potential danger.

transcript.speaker: Pippa
transcript.text: Some cars do this with animations – displays of moving images.

transcript.speaker: Pippa
transcript.text: For example, a green man walking to signal it's safe to cross.

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: Animations alert pedestrians but are not suitable for runners and cyclists, who are travelling too fast to react.

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: They only have time for a glance.

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: A glance at something means a quick look.

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: So, instead Stephen's team used coloured light rings, similar to traffic lights, to warn cyclists and runners.

transcript.speaker: Pippa
transcript.text: Culture is another problem.

transcript.speaker: Pippa
transcript.text: The meaning of body language can change.

transcript.speaker: Pippa
transcript.text: For example, hand waving can mean 'please proceed' in one culture, but 'thank you' in another.

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: Ammar Al-Taie is a researcher at the Advanced Institute of Science and Technology in South Korea.

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: Here, Ammar tells BBC World Service's Tech Life why Korean culture is especially suited to self-driving cars.

transcript.speaker: Ammar Al-Taie
transcript.text: In South Korea, for example, jaywalking is illegal, whereas in the UK, you know, we tend to jaywalk a lot.

transcript.speaker: Pippa
transcript.text: Jaywalking is an American English word.

transcript.speaker: Pippa
transcript.text: It means crossing the road at a place where crossing is not allowed or without taking care.

transcript.speaker: Pippa
transcript.text: Unlike Britain, jaywalking is rare in South Korea, making the country safer for autonomous cars.

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: We've heard a lot about making driverless cars safer, and with plans to introduce them to London later this year, we'll soon see how safe they really are.

transcript.speaker: Pippa
transcript.text: Now, isn't it time to reveal the answer to your question, Phil?

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: I asked you which city was the first to have self-driving cars on the road, and you said it was Phoenix... and that is the correct answer.

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: Phoenix, Arizona, was the first city in the world to have self-driving cars operating on public roads without a human safety driver, and that was in 2017.

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: Let's recap the vocabulary we've learned, starting with eye contact – looking directly into someone's eyes.

transcript.speaker: Pippa
transcript.text: To wave at someone is a way of saying hi, by raising your hand and waving it from side to side.

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: If you alert someone, you warn them of potential danger.

transcript.speaker: Pippa
transcript.text: An animation is a display made up of moving images.

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: A glance is a quick, brief look at something.

transcript.speaker: Pippa
transcript.text: And finally, the American English term jaywalking means crossing the road where you're not supposed to.

transcript.speaker: Pippa
transcript.text: Once again, our six minutes are up.

transcript.speaker: Pippa
transcript.text: If you'd like to hear more programmes about technology, you'll find plenty on our tech topic page, all on our website.

transcript.speaker: Pippa
transcript.text: And there you'll also find a quiz and worksheet for this episode.

transcript.speaker: Pippa
transcript.text: Visit bbclearningenglish.com.

transcript.speaker: Pippa
transcript.text: We'll see you again soon, but for now it's goodbye.

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: Goodbye!

listening.task: 출근길 운전하면서 한 번은 대략적인 내용만 듣고, 저녁에 두 번째는 스크립트를 보면서 들어요. 그다음 퀴즈에 답해 보세요. 'eye contact', 'alert', 'glance', 'jaywalking'이 나오는 부분을 잘 들어 보세요.

quiz.q: Which was the first city to have fully driverless robotaxis on the streets? a) Philadelphia, b) Phoenix, c) San Francisco
quiz.answer: b) Phoenix. 2017년 미국 애리조나주 Phoenix에서 안전요원 없이 자율주행차가 처음 공공도로를 달렸어요. Pippa가 맞혔어요!

reading.title: Climate change is making some African deserts greener
reading.source: The Economist (public reprint via Hindustan Times)
reading.summaryKo: 한때 90%까지 줄어 '기후 붕괴의 상징'이던 아프리카 차드호(Lake Chad)가 2012년 이후 수면 면적이 두 배 이상 늘었어요. 사하라 남쪽 사헬 지역은 비가 많아져 땅이 다시 초록으로 변하고 있지만, 그만큼 홍수 피해도 커지고 있어요. 문제는 아프리카의 기후가 '더 습해질지 더 건조해질지' 방향조차 예측하기 어렵다는 것. 기상 관측소가 세계의 10%뿐이고 그마저 절반은 데이터가 부정확해서, 결국 '더 많고 더 좋은 데이터'가 적응의 첫걸음이래요. 어제 통계 기사와도 이어지는 주제예요.
excerpt: For decades Lake Chad seemed to be a terrifying portent of climate collapse. Yet years of punishing droughts helped to shrink it by as much as 90%.
Instead the opposite happened. Today Lake Chad has more water than it has had for decades.
reading.tip: 'Instead the opposite happened.'처럼 짧은 문장으로 예상을 뒤집는 게 Economist의 전형적인 전개예요. 'seemed destined to ~'(~할 운명처럼 보였다), 'a grim preview of ~'(~의 암울한 예고편) 같은 표현도 눈여겨보세요.

vocab.example: Usually, a driver makes eye contact with me.
It's important to alert people to driverless cars.
Cyclists only have time for a glance.
In South Korea, jaywalking is illegal.
Lake Chad seemed to be a terrifying portent of climate collapse.
How climate change will play out across Africa is deeply uncertain.
Helping Africans adapt to shifts that are hard to predict is a priority.
